summary.suggested: The St. Louis Post-Dispatch reported that Allen's daughter, Mrs. Mary Taylor, was twice refused leave to see him at the Baptist Hospital, and said her mother was alive in Birmingham and that Mrs. Hartgrove had taken charge of his money.

metadata.notes: Masthead: Monday, St. Louis Post-Dispatch, March 30, 1903, page 6, column 1. The current summary mentions an 'open letter'; the article says a statement to the Post-Dispatch.

facts.fact: Allen's daughter, Mrs. Mary Taylor, was refused admittance to him at his rooms over the saloon and twice at the Baptist Hospital
places: Baptist Hospital, Garrison and Franklin avenues, St. Louis

facts.fact: Allen's doctor diagnosed pneumonia and Allen was moved to the Baptist Hospital at Garrison and Franklin avenues on Saturday
places: Baptist Hospital, Garrison and Franklin avenues, St. Louis

facts.fact: Mrs. Taylor said her mother and sister were living in Birmingham, England
Mrs. Taylor said Mrs. Hartgrove had assumed power of attorney and took charge of the money in the saloon's cash register
Mrs. Taylor put the case in the hands of attorney Frank A. C. MacManus, an old friend of her father, to gain access to him by law

notes: The claim that Mrs. Hartgrove has a husband in Kansas City whom she is suing for divorce matches an index line with id 000, so it is not repeated as a fact here. This contradicts article 197's claim that Allen was a widower and that her first husband was dead.
